strengths: A novel and well-motivated synthetic data generation pipeline (CAUKER) that successfully combines Gaussian Process kernels (for local temporal properties) with Structural Causal Models (for complex, clustering-friendly relationships), specifically designed for classification TSFMs.

A comprehensive and insightful analysis of scaling laws (data, model size, and training time) in zero-shot time series classification, highlighting that synthetic data leads to clean monotonic scaling while real-world datasets often suffer from irregular/flat scaling.

Strong empirical results on a standard benchmark (128 UCR datasets) using two representative foundation model architectures (Mantis and MOMENT), demonstrating that pretraining on CAUKER can match or exceed the performance of models pretrained on massive real-world corpora, with significantly higher sample efficiency.

Good qualitative and representation analysis using UMAP projections, CKA similarity, and non-linearity metrics to explain why the CAUKER synthetic data helps models learn generalizable and robust features.
weaknesses: There are a few writing and referencing errors: Section 4.5 refers to 'Table 6' which does not exist (the results are actually shown in the table at the top of Figure 6 on page 10).
Section C.1 in the Appendix is titled 'Pseudocode of the CAUKER' but does not actually contain any formal pseudocode or algorithm box, only a high-level paragraph description.
The details of the random DAG generation in Step 5 (e.g., how the topology, number of nodes $V$, and edge count $E$ are sampled) are somewhat vague, which could affect exact reproducibility.

strengths: The core idea of pretraining classification Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) purely on synthetic data is highly practical, scalable, and helps mitigate data curation and leakage issues.

The hybrid approach of combining Gaussian Process (GP) kernels (to model temporal motifs like seasonality/trends) with Structural Causal Models (to capture non-linear, multi-variable interactions) is conceptually sound.

Comprehensive empirical analysis is conducted using two state-of-the-art models (Mantis and MOMENT) with different training paradigms (contrastive learning vs. masked reconstruction) across 128 UCR datasets.
The study of data and model scaling laws under synthetic vs. real-world pretraining settings provides valuable insights, illustrating that synthetic data yields more consistent scaling behaviors.
weaknesses: Severe draft/formatting issues: In Section 4.5, the text references "Table 6" ("From the results presented in Table 6, we note..."), but Table 6 does not exist in the document. The table containing these results appears to be embedded inside Figure 6 on page 10.

Missing promised content: Section C.1 of the Appendix is titled "Pseudocode of the CAUKER" and the text on page 5 states "A complete pseudocode of this procedure... are provided in Appendix C". However, Section C.1 contains only a short descriptive paragraph and absolutely no pseudocode block. This is a critical omission for reproducibility.

Unfair/Unclear baseline comparison: In Figure 6, the "Mantis dataset" (1.89M) baseline achieves 78.66% but includes UCR train samples (data leakage for this zero-shot setting), while CAUKER (100K) achieves 78.55% without UCR. To show a fair out-of-distribution (OOD) comparison, the authors should have trained Mantis on a version of the real-world dataset that excludes the UCR target data, rather than comparing a leaked baseline to an unleaked one.

The mathematical details in Section 3.2 (Step 5, Causal Graph Propagation) are somewhat vague. It is unclear how the linear layer and concatenation step operate over variable-length nodes, and how the interpolation step is structured during generation.
No code repository or implementation code has been provided, which, combined with the missing pseudocode, severely limits the reproducibility of the CAUKER generation pipeline.

strengths: The paper addresses a very important and timely problem: pretraining Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) using purely synthetic data, which circumvents the costly and privacy-sensitive process of real-world data curation.

The proposed CAUKER algorithm introduces a novel integration of Gaussian Process (GP) kernel compositions (capturing localized time-series patterns like seasonality and trends) and Structural Causal Models (SCMs) (introducing complex causal dependencies and cluster structures), making it highly suitable for classification pretraining.

The paper presents a comprehensive and insightful study on scaling laws (evaluating both data scale and model scale) for classification TSFMs, illustrating that synthetic pretraining datasets show clear power-law scaling whereas real-world datasets (like UEA) can show irregular or non-monotonic scaling.

The empirical results are strong: models pretrained on CAUKER data are highly sample-efficient, requiring significantly fewer samples to match the zero-shot downstream classification performance of models pretrained on massive real-world collections.
weaknesses: There is a discrepancy regarding the pseudocode. The text on page 5 states: 'A complete pseudocode of this procedure... are provided in Appendix C.' However, Appendix C.1 only contains a single paragraph of textual description and does not contain any pseudocode or algorithm box.

There are several incorrect cross-references to tables and figures. For instance, Section 4.5 references 'Table 6', but no Table 6 exists in the paper (it appears to refer to the table embedded within Figure 6 on page 10). Similarly, Section 4.2.2 refers to 'Figure 9', which is located in Appendix G (page 21) rather than the main text, making the reading flow difficult.

It is not entirely clear how the 'clustering structure' or 'classes' are mathematically formulated during the synthetic generation process for CAUKER. While the authors state that CAUKER generates sequences with cluster structures appropriate for classification, the SCM step (Step 5) generates nodes of a DAG. It is unclear how distinct classes/clusters are assigned or partitioned during contrastive or masked pretraining without hand-crafting specific parameter sets (as done in Appendix G for visualization).

For the baseline pretraining on the multivariate UEA dataset, the authors split multivariate channels into individual univariate series. While necessary because Mantis/MOMENT are univariate encoders, this channel-independent treatment likely destroys cross-channel temporal correlations, which might explain the poor scaling and performance of the UEA baseline. A comparison with a natively univariate real-world pretraining corpus would make the baseline comparison fairer.

strengths: Compelling and highly practical motivation: obtaining large-scale real-world classification data for pre-training time series foundation models (TSFMs) is challenging. Showing that synthetic data can serve as an efficient surrogate is a highly valuable contribution.

Well-conceived methodology: the combination of Gaussian Processes (providing temporal features like trends and seasonality) and Structural Causal Models (introducing causal structure and class-conditional clustering) is well-reasoned and elegant.

Thorough and rigorous evaluation: the authors evaluate their method using two prominent classification TSFMs (Mantis and MOMENT) across various data sizes and model architectures, showing that pre-training on CAUKER matches or exceeds real-data pre-training performance.

Insightful exploration of scaling laws: the analysis of data and model scaling laws is well-executed, revealing that synthetic pre-training yields smooth and monotonic scaling behavior, unlike real-world corpora which suffer from domain mismatch and limited diversity.

Excellent generalization: evaluations are extended to out-of-distribution scenarios (WOODS), clinical irregular multivariate series (P12, P19), and even forecasting (Chronos), proving the versatility of the proposed synthetic dataset.
weaknesses: Terminology clarification: the evaluation setup is referred to as 'zero-shot classification,' but it involves training a Random Forest or SVM on the downstream training set with frozen representations. This is more accurately described as 'linear/shallow probing' or 'frozen representation evaluation.'

Pre-training is limited to univariate settings: while the SCM naturally produces multivariate dependencies, the pre-training experiments are restricted to univariate trajectories to align with current TSFM architectures. A deeper discussion or exploration of multivariate pre-training would enhance the work.

Scalability of dataset generation: while the authors show that CAUKER is faster than KernelSynth for 1K samples, generating very large datasets (e.g., 10M samples) could still introduce significant CPU/GPU overhead. More details on the computational requirements for the larger-scale generations would be beneficial.

strengths: A novel and well-motivated synthetic data generation framework (CAUKER) that effectively combines Gaussian Process kernel composition with Structural Causal Models (SCMs) specifically for pre-training classification time series foundation models.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation showing that pre-training on CAUKER synthetic data matches or exceeds the zero-shot performance of models trained on much larger, curated real-world corpora (e.g., 100K CAUKER vs. 1.89M real-world samples for Mantis).

A systematic and highly insightful study of data and model scaling laws in time series classification, demonstrating that synthetic data exhibits robust and clean scaling behavior, whereas real-world datasets like UEA show irregular or flat scaling due to lack of diversity.

Strong generalizability demonstrated across different model architectures (Mantis and MOMENT), learning paradigms (contrastive and masked reconstruction), tasks (classification and forecasting with Chronos), and out-of-distribution benchmarks (WOODS and clinical datasets).
Excellent writing quality, clear structure, and highly thorough appendices including complete pseudocode, parameter analyses, qualitative visualizations, and computational efficiency breakdowns.
weaknesses: The paper would benefit from a more intuitive explanation of how the Structural Causal Model (SCM) structure translates to better representation learning when the models are pre-trained on univariate sequences individually. Specifically, explaining how SCM-generated trajectories form natural clusters/families that directly benefit contrastive or masked pre-training objectives would improve clarity.

The evaluation on forecasting (using Chronos) is an interesting extension, but it remains a bit brief. More discussion on whether the SCM causal graph propagation helps forecasting models learn better temporal dynamics compared to pure GP-based models (like KernelSynth) would strengthen this section.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and timely challenge: pre-training time series foundation models (TSFMs) for classification tasks using purely synthetic data, mitigating data collection costs and leakage issues.

The proposed CAUKER pipeline elegantly combines Gaussian Process (GP) kernel composition (to capture realistic temporal dynamics like trends and seasonality) with Structural Causal Models (SCMs) to generate complex, causally coherent class structures.

It provides a thorough and pioneering study of scaling laws in time series classification (examining dataset size, model capacity, and training compute), revealing that real-world benchmarks often fail to scale monotonically due to domain mismatch and lack of diversity, whereas CAUKER synthetic data scales beautifully.

The empirical evaluation is highly comprehensive, covering 128 UCR datasets, the WOODS benchmark, and clinical datasets (P12, P19) across two distinct foundation model architectures (Mantis and MOMENT).
Exceptional sample efficiency is demonstrated: pre-training on just 100K synthetic CAUKER series achieves performance almost identical to pre-training on up to 1.89M real-world sequences.

The paper is very well-written, with rich qualitative analyses including CKA representation analysis, PCA projections, attention rollout maps, and even an extension showing competitive zero-shot forecasting performance on Chronos.
weaknesses: The individual building blocks (GP kernel compositions and SCMs) are largely drawn from existing work (KernelSynth and TabPFN), making the technical assembly of the pipeline somewhat incremental, although their unification is highly principled and well-motivated for classification.
In Table 1, the performance gain of CAUKER over the Mean-KernelSynth baseline is relatively small for Mantis (78.31% vs 78.20%), though the margin is more pronounced for MOMENT.

The use of the term 'zero-shot' to describe representation learning evaluation with an SVM/RF classifier trained on the target domain's training set (essentially linear probing) might be slightly confusing to researchers outside the time series domain, although the authors clearly define their protocol in Section 3.1.
